subject: Critical Thinking
title: Decision Journals: Learning from Your Own Track Record
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Decision Journals: Learning from Your Own Track Record.

hook.text: Ray Dalio keeps a decision journal. Before each decision, he writes down his reasoning.

buildup.text: A decision journal records: what you decided, why, what alternatives you considered, and what you expected to happen.

discovery.text: Months later, you review. Were your reasons sound? Were your predictions accurate? What did you miss?

twist.text: Without a journal, hindsight bias rewrites your memory.

climax.text: The journal separates decision quality from outcome quality.

quiz.question: Why is a decision journal valuable?
options: It records reasoning before hindsight bias rewrites your memory

details.summary: A decision journal records your reasoning, confidence level, and expectations before outcomes are known. Reviewing it later reveals systematic biases in your thinking that memory alone would distort or erase.
details.whyItMatters: Without a written record, hindsight bias rewrites your memories of past decisions. A journal provides honest feedback that memory cannot.
takeaways: Write down predictions and reasoning before outcomes are known
Review past entries to detect personal biases and patterns
Decision journals combat hindsight bias and overconfidence

faq.question: What should you include in a decision journal entry?
faq.answer: Record the decision, the alternatives considered, your confidence level as a percentage, the reasoning behind your choice, what you expect to happen, and what factors might prove you wrong. Keep it brief but honest.

faq.question: How often should you review your decision journal for maximum benefit?
faq.answer: Review quarterly or whenever enough outcomes have resolved. Look for patterns: are you consistently overconfident? Do you neglect certain types of risk? The journal works only if you revisit it honestly.
